title: Next year's text
hookLine: choose what you'll study next: a book of Tanakh, a tractate, a code
tomorrow: why would the Talmud threaten people who study alone?

cards: A stack of maybe-someday books on a nightstand, the top one with its bookmark stuck near the start. Choosing what to read next can stall a person for months.
Avot de-Rabbi Natan tells of a grown man named Akiva who had never learned anything at all. One day, by a well, he sees a stone with a hollow worn into it. Who carved this, he asks.
Water, they tell him. The water that falls on it, day after day.

teach.b: Akiva thinks: if soft water can hollow hard stone, words of Torah can carve a place in my heart, which is only flesh and blood. So he goes with his young son, and the two of them sit down before a teacher of children.
And what does a grown man read first? The alef-bet. Letters.
Then, the story says, Torat Kohanim, the book of Leviticus, and on and on, until he had learned the whole Torah.

Here's the line to tell a friend tonight: a midrash says children once began the Torah not with Genesis but with Leviticus, the laws of offerings, because, it says, the pure should come and study what is pure.
So what's next year's text? The tradition offers real choices.

teach.h: A BOOK, A TRACTATE, A CODE.
teach.b: A book of Tanakh, read slowly. A tractate of Talmud. A code, like the laws Maimonides gathered.
The choice matters less than the dripping. Pick the one you'll actually open, again and again, until it wears a place in you. Akiva chose the alef-bet, beside his son.
Nobody would call it the hardest text. It was the right one.

how: Jewish adults often choose a text to study for a season or a year: a book of the Tanakh, a tractate of Talmud, or a section of a code such as Maimonides' Mishneh Torah, alone, with a partner or in a class.

o: a book you finish before the new year begins
the reading a synagogue assigns each new year
the text you choose to study in the year ahead

s: Akiva started with the hardest text he could find

games.q: your aunt, in her fifties, wants to start studying Torah but is embarrassed to begin with a beginner's book. what does Akiva's story suggest?
o: start at the beginning, unashamed; Akiva sat down with the children.
skip the basics; at her age, start with something advanced.
it's too late; Akiva's story is really a story about children.
games.why: Akiva, a grown man, sat beside his son before a children's teacher and began with the alef-bet.

practice: Pick up one book near you, or open one on a screen: something you've meant to read. Hold it, look at it, and read its first line slowly. Then ask one question: is this the text I'd open again and again next year?

wordCard.voice: Next year's text: the one book you choose to study in the year ahead, a book of Tanakh, a tractate, a code, opened again and again like water on stone.

orig.note: Hebrew: the alphabet, named for its letters alef and bet; Akiva's first lesson.

carryVoice: Something to keep: choose next year's text. Drip by drip, it wears a place in you. Until next time.

sources.ref: Avot de-Rabbi Natan, version A, chapter 6 (Akiva sees the stone hollowed by water; learns with his son before a children's teacher: the alef-bet, Torat Kohanim, until the whole Torah)
Vayikra Rabbah 7:3 (why young children begin with Torat Kohanim: let the pure come and occupy themselves with the pure)
